kernels.name: mul_mat_q (MMQ)

launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D: (1, block_num_y, block_num_x) * (1, nwarps, WARP_SIZE). block_num_x = (ncols_x + mmq_x - 1) / mmq_x, block_num_y = (nrows_x + mmq_y - 1) / mmq_y
launch_config.notes: Work-group size of 64 is well below the recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. The WARP_SIZE=16 matches native SIMD width, but nwarps=4 gives only 4 sub-groups per work-group. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] is a correctness risk since the entire kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as the sub-group width.

strided_accesses: X-tile loads have row-stride separation (different rows of the tile separated by blocks_per_row in global memory)
Y-tile loads have per-warp column strides as each warp loads a different column block
memory_patterns.notes: All loads use scalar 4-byte get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned helpers. No sycl::vec or 16-byte loads. Within a sub-group, consecutive lanes read consecutive data from the qs field of quantization blocks, which is reasonably coalesced.

slm_usage.notes: SLM usage is 3-5 KB depending on quantization format, vastly underutilizing the 64 KB available per Xe-core. Bank conflict avoidance uses CUDA-style +1 stride padding (WARP_SIZE+1=17 stride), which may actually cause conflicts on Intel's 16-bank SLM architecture. tile_x_ql, tile_x_dm/tile_x_d, tile_x_sc, tile_x_qh (format-dependent), tile_y_qs, tile_y_ds are allocated.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction needed — each thread accumulates into its own private sum[2][1] and writes a unique output element. This is architecturally correct for the tiling approach.

data_types.notes: Primary compute is integer dot products (dp4a on int8/uint8 quantized values) scaled by float/half factors. Accumulation in float32 is appropriate for numerical stability. joint_matrix could replace dp4a with XMX hardware int8 matmul for significant throughput gains.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions used. All compute is integer bitwise ops, dp4a, and float multiply-add.

hot_loops: Outer K-tiling loop (line 1228): iterates blocks_per_row_x / blocks_per_warp times, NOT unrolled — trip count is data-dependent
qr loop (line 1236): iterates qr times (2 for most formats), UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Inner k loop (line 1289-1301): iterates WARP_SIZE/(qr*vdr) times (1-2 iterations), NOT unrolled due to register pressure (comment on line 1289)
Inner j loop (line 1291): mmq_x/nwarps = 1 iteration, UNROLLED — trivially 1 iteration
Inner i loop (line 1293): mmq_y/WARP_SIZE = 2 iterations, UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Load tile loops: 8 iterations each, all UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
loop_analysis.notes: The critical hot inner k-loop is explicitly NOT unrolled due to register pressure (comment says unrolling causes too much register pressure). With the current tiny tile sizes, the inner loop body is only 1-2 iterations. Increasing tile sizes would require revisiting unroll strategy.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: With mmq_x=4 and mmq_y=32, each work-group computes only a 32x4 output tile, resulting in very low arithmetic intensity per memory load. The tiny work-group size (64) also means poor occupancy on Xe2 hardware. The kernel is compute-limited by the lack of XMX utilization — dp4a provides far lower throughput than XMX joint_matrix operations.
anti_patterns: CRITICAL: Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] — kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as sub-group width but doesn't enforce it. Compiler may choose SIMD8 or SIMD32, breaking correctness
CUDA-style SLM bank conflict padding (+1 stride) mismatched for Intel 16-bank SLM
Very small work-group size (64) — well below recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs
Tiny tile sizes (mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32) wasting SLM capacity and limiting compute density
3D nd_range with unused first dimension (always 1) — should be 2D
DPCT migration artifacts: __dpct_inline__, DPCT warning comments, dpct::dp4a calls
CUDA architecture naming (AMPERE, PASCAL, RDNA1/RDNA2) mapped to Intel Gen labels with TODO comments
Manual warp/lane indexing via get_local_id instead of SYCL sub-group APIs
No vectorized memory loads — all scalar 4-byte loads
Massive code duplication: 10 formats x 2 (need_check) = 20 near-identical kernel launches (~1200 lines)

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to the kernel. The entire kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as the sub-group size for indexing, SLM layout, and tile computation. Without this attribute, the compiler may select SIMD8 or SIMD32, potentially breaking correctness. This is a correctness fix first, performance second.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness guarantee. May also improve performance by ensuring the compiler generates SIMD16 code matching the kernel's assumptions. Low single-digit percent speedup from removing compiler ambiguity.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to the lambda in the parallel_for calls (20 launch sites across all formats). Must be placed on the kernel lambda, not a device function.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: This is a correctness fix. Risk is if the kernel actually performs better at a different sub-group size, but the logic requires SIMD16.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 64 to 256 by increasing nwarps from 4 to 16, or by increasing tile dimensions. Current 64-thread work-groups severely underutilize Intel GPU hardware which prefers 256-512. With 64 threads, each Xe-core can run 64/64=1 work-group max per hardware thread slot, leading to poor latency hiding.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement from better occupancy and latency hiding. More sub-groups per work-group means better utilization of the Xe-core's 8 XVEs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Increase mmq_y to 128 (from 32) and/or mmq_x to 16 (from 4), with nwarps=16. This increases the output tile to 128x16, improving arithmetic intensity. Must also increase SLM allocation proportionally (from ~4KB to ~16-32KB, still well within 64KB limit). Register pressure needs profiling — the inner k-loop unrolling comment may need revisiting.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Larger tiles increase register pressure. The existing comment about unrolling causing register pressure suggests this dimension is sensitive. Needs careful tuning and benchmarking per quantization format.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace scalar dpct::dp4a() calls with joint_matrix (XMX) operations for the integer dot product inner loop. The B60 has 160 XMX engines that provide ~197 Int8 TOPS vs the ~12 TFLOPS of scalar FP32. The inner loop computes int8 dot products that map directly to XMX's int8->int32 matmul capability.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 4-8x throughput improvement for the compute-bound inner loop. XMX provides 16x the peak int8 throughput vs scalar paths, but memory access overhead and tile management limit real-world gains.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Use sycl::ext::oneapi::experimental::matrix::joint_matrix with int8 inputs and int32 accumulator. Requires restructuring the tile loading to match XMX tile sizes (M=8, N=16, K=32 for int8 on Xe2). The quantized data is already in int8 format in SLM, so the primary work is reshaping the data flow. Requires [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] as a prerequisite.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Major kernel rewrite. joint_matrix has strict layout requirements that may not align well with the varied quantization formats (q4_0 through q6_K each have different block structures). May need format-specific XMX tile loaders. Risk of numerical differences in accumulation order.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 16-byte loads (sycl::vec<int,4>) instead of scalar 4-byte loads in the tile loading functions. Adjacent work-items currently each load one 4-byte int; instead, each work-item could load a vec4 (16 bytes), reducing the number of memory transactions by 4x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-25% improvement in tile loading phase bandwidth utilization. Impact depends on what fraction of kernel time is spent in loads vs compute.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned with reinterpret_cast<sycl::vec<int,4>*> aligned loads where quantization block layout permits. Must ensure 16-byte alignment of source data. The load_tiles_* functions (10 format-specific) each need modification.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements may not always be met depending on quantization block sizes. Some formats (IQ types) have irregular layouts. Need to handle edge cases where the remaining data is less than 16 bytes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix SLM bank conflict avoidance for Intel GPU architecture. Current code uses CUDA-style +1 padding (stride WARP_SIZE+1=17) for SLM arrays. Intel SLM has 16 banks with 4-byte granularity. With stride 17, consecutive row accesses hit banks 0,17%16=1,34%16=2,... which is actually conflict-free for row access but may conflict for column access patterns. Analyze actual access patterns and adjust padding for Intel's 16-bank layout.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement in SLM-heavy phases if bank conflicts exist. Requires profiling to quantify actual conflict rate.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace (WARP_SIZE + 1) stride with a stride that avoids conflicts for the actual access patterns in vec_dot_* functions. For Intel's 16 banks, a stride of 17 (WARP_SIZE+1) actually works well for sequential row access but may need adjustment for the interleaved access pattern in the dot product phase. Profile with Intel VTune or Level Zero metrics to measure actual SLM bank conflicts before and after.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: SLM padding changes are localized. Can be benchmarked independently. Low risk of correctness issues.

optimization_opportunities.description: Tune tile configuration per quantization format instead of using one-size-fits-all mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32 for all formats. Different quantization formats have different memory footprints and compute intensities. For example, q4_0 (4-bit, simple) could use larger tiles than q6_K (6-bit, complex scales) without exceeding register or SLM limits.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement for some formats by better matching tile sizes to format complexity.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: The configuration macros already support per-format tile sizes (MMQ_X_Q4_0_AMPERE, etc.). Change the Intel target configuration from the current uniform mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32 to format-specific values. Simpler formats (q4_0, q4_1, q8_0) can use larger tiles; complex formats (q3_K, q5_K, q6_K) may need smaller tiles to avoid register spilling.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires per-format benchmarking. Wrong tile sizes can cause register spilling and severe performance regressions.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace item_ct1.barrier() with item_ct1.barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space) since the barriers only synchronize SLM accesses, not global memory. This tells the hardware that only local memory fence is needed, potentially reducing barrier overhead.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% improvement. Barriers are executed twice per qr iteration, so the effect compounds but is still minor.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change the two barrier() calls in the mul_mat_q template (lines ~1287 and ~1312) to barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space). Verify that no global memory synchronization is actually needed between the barrier points.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: If any global memory accesses actually depend on the barrier (e.g., the output write at the end), this would be incorrect. Analysis shows the barriers are only for SLM coherence, so local_space fence should suffice.

optimization_opportunities.description: Investigate whether the hot inner k-loop (line ~1289) can be partially unrolled now that the target is Intel GPU (different register file characteristics than NVIDIA). The comment says unrolling causes too much register pressure, but this was likely profiled on NVIDIA hardware. Intel Xe2 has 512 bytes GRF per thread in SIMD16 mode.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% if register pressure permits. The k-loop has only 1-2 iterations for most formats, so full unroll would eliminate the loop overhead entirely.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Try adding #pragma unroll to the k-loop for simple formats (q4_0, q8_0) first. Monitor register usage via -cl-intel-greater-than-4GB-buffer-required or IGC internal flags. If registers spill, revert.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Register spilling on Intel GPUs causes performance cliffs (spill to SLM or global memory). Must benchmark each format individually.

kernels.efficiency_notes: This is a DPCT-migrated kernel running with CUDA-optimized tile sizes (optimized for NVIDIA Ampere with warp size 32, then scaled down to warp size 16). The work-group size of 64 is far below Intel's preferred 256-512. No XMX utilization despite having 160 XMX engines. Scalar dp4a instead of hardware matrix multiply. Minimal SLM utilization (3-5 KB of 64 KB available). No vectorized loads. The kernel functions correctly but is leaving substantial performance on the table.

kernels.name: mul_mat_vec_q (MMVQ)

launch_config.global_size_expression: Legacy: (1, 1, ceil(nrows/MMV_Y)) * (1, 1, WARP_SIZE). Reordered: (1, 1, block_num_y * WARP_SIZE) with WG=(1, 1, num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE)
launch_config.notes: Two distinct launch patterns: legacy kernels (used for 17 of 20 formats) have a work-group size of only 16 (1 sub-group), which is far below Intel's recommended 256-512. Reordered kernels (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K only) use 256 work-items (16 sub-groups per work-group), which is properly tuned. GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y=1 means only 1 row per sub-group. All launches correctly specify [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]].

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Legacy kernels use AoS (array-of-structures) block layout where adjacent sub-group lanes read different offsets within the same quantization block — not truly coalesced across blocks. Reordered kernels use SoA (structure-of-arrays) layout with contiguous quants separated from scales, providing much better coalescing.
strided_accesses: Legacy: x[ibx] indexed by row*blocks_per_row + i — AoS layout means quantization block fields (qs, d, qh, sc) are interleaved, causing strided access to each field
Legacy: y[iby] indexed similarly with interleaved q8_1 block fields
memory_patterns.notes: All loads use scalar 4-byte helpers: get_int_from_uint8() reconstructs ints from bytes, get_int_from_int8_aligned() does direct 4-byte cast. No sycl::vec types for memory loads. The reordered kernels access contiguous quant/scale regions via separated pointers, which is more bandwidth-efficient.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM (shared local memory) is used by any MMVQ kernel variant. All communication is done via sub-group shuffles (dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor in legacy, sycl::reduce_over_group in reordered). This means the Y vector data — shared across all sub-groups in a work-group — is redundantly loaded from global memory by each sub-group in the reordered kernels.

reduction_pattern.reduction_details: Legacy: manual butterfly reduction via dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor (DPCT artifact of CUDA __shfl_xor_sync), #pragma unroll for log2(WARP_SIZE)=4 iterations. Reordered: proper sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, std::plus<>()). Each sub-group reduces its partial dot product to a single scalar for one output row.

data_types.notes: FP32 accumulation is appropriate for numerical stability. Integer dp4a for quantized dot products. Optional GGML_SYCL_F16 build flag enables half-precision scale arithmetic in some vec_dot functions. joint_matrix is not directly applicable to matrix-vector (single vector) but could be used if multiple vectors were batched.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions. All compute is integer bitwise ops, dp4a, and float multiply-add.

hot_loops: Main block loop (line ~80): iterates blocks_per_row/blocks_per_warp times, NOT unrolled (dynamic trip count based on ncols)
Inner elem loop (line ~84): iterates qi/vdr/WARP_SIZE times — typically 0 or 1 iterations for most formats, NOT unrolled in legacy (but IS unrolled in reordered kernels)
Reduction loop (line ~93): log2(WARP_SIZE)=4 iterations, UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
vecdotq.hpp inner loops: all short constant-trip-count loops with #pragma unroll (e.g., QR2_K=4, QR4_K=2 iterations)
loop_analysis.notes: Inner loops in vecdotq.hpp are properly unrolled. The main block loop cannot be unrolled (dynamic). The reordered kernels are better optimized with #pragma unroll on the inner element loop.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Matrix-vector multiplication is inherently memory-bandwidth bound: each weight element is loaded once and used for exactly one multiply-add (arithmetic intensity ~0.5 ops/byte for Q4 formats). The B60's compute intensity threshold is ~27 ops/byte, so MMVQ is far below — it needs maximum memory bandwidth utilization. The legacy kernel's 16-thread work-group and AoS layout hurt bandwidth efficiency.
anti_patterns: Legacy kernels: work-group size of 16 (1 sub-group) — far below Intel's recommended 256-512, poor occupancy and latency hiding
Legacy kernels: manual butterfly shuffle reduction (dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor) instead of sycl::reduce_over_group — DPCT artifact
DPCT artifacts throughout: dpct::dp4a, dpct::vectorized_binary, dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor, __dpct_inline__, DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP guards
3D nd_range with 2 unused dimensions (both dim0 and dim1 are trivially 1) — should be 1D
No SLM caching of Y vector — in reordered kernels with 16 sub-groups, each sub-group redundantly loads the same Y data from global memory (16x bandwidth waste for Y)
No vectorized loads — all scalar 4-byte loads via get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned
Reorder support limited to 3 of 20 quantization formats (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K) — other formats stuck with legacy AoS layout
Massive code duplication: 10 IQ-specific kernel functions nearly identical to the generic mul_mat_vec_q template (~430 lines of duplicate code)
~20 nearly-identical launcher functions differing only in template parameters (~500 lines)

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase legacy kernel work-group size from 16 to 256 by adopting the reordered kernel's multi-sub-group pattern (16 sub-groups per work-group). Currently 17 of 20 formats use the legacy launch with only 16 work-items per work-group, resulting in severely underutilized Intel GPU hardware. Each sub-group still computes one row independently, but grouping 16 sub-groups into one work-group enables better scheduling and occupancy.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 25-50% throughput improvement from better occupancy and memory-level parallelism. This is the single highest-impact optimization for MMVQ on Intel GPUs. The reordered kernel paths already demonstrate this pattern works correctly.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change the legacy launcher from block_dims=(1,1,WARP_SIZE) to block_dims=(1,1,num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE) with num_subgroups=16. Adjust block_nums accordingly: block_num_z = ceil(nrows / (GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y * num_subgroups)). Each sub-group uses its sub-group ID to compute a different row. The reordered kernels (lines 537-554) serve as the template.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The reordered kernels already prove this pattern works for Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K. The same pattern is straightforward to apply to all other formats since sub-groups are independent. Only risk is if nrows is not a multiple of 16 — need bounds checking (already present in the kernel via row < nrows guard).

optimization_opportunities.description: Cache Y vector data in SLM for the multi-sub-group work-groups. In the reordered kernels (and the proposed multi-sub-group legacy kernels), all 16 sub-groups in a work-group iterate over the same Y vector. Currently each sub-group independently loads Y from global memory, wasting 16x bandwidth on Y. By loading Y once per work-group into SLM and sharing it, Y-related global memory traffic drops by ~16x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% overall throughput improvement for memory-bound MMVQ. Y vector is typically ncols/QK8_1 blocks of 36 bytes each. For a 4096-column matrix with Q4_0: ncols/32 * 36 = 4608 bytes — easily fits in the 64KB SLM budget.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Allocate sycl::local_accessor for Y data. Have sub-group 0 (or all sub-groups cooperatively) load Y into SLM. Insert group_barrier(). Then all sub-groups read Y from SLM instead of global memory. For the main loop, load the next tile of Y data in a double-buffered fashion to overlap global loads with SLM reads.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adds SLM pressure and barriers. For very large ncols, Y may not fit in SLM entirely — need tiled loading. The barrier overhead must not exceed the bandwidth savings. For small nrows (few sub-groups active), the benefit diminishes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace all 10 instances of manual dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reduction in legacy kernels with sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, sycl::plus<float>()). The reordered kernels already use the correct SYCL idiom. The manual shuffle reduction is a DPCT artifact and may not compile to optimal code on Intel GPUs.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% improvement. The compiler may generate better reduction code from the high-level reduce_over_group API than from the manual butterfly pattern. More importantly, it removes a DPCT dependency.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In each of the 10 IQ-variant kernels and the generic mul_mat_vec_q, replace the '#pragma unroll for (mask = WARP_SIZE/2; ...) { tmp += dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor(sg, tmp, mask); }' with 'tmp = sycl::reduce_over_group(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, sycl::plus<float>());'. Alternatively, use the existing warp_reduce_sum() helper from common.hpp.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Direct replacement with standard SYCL API. The reordered kernels already prove this works correctly. No algorithmic change — same mathematical result.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 8-byte or 16-byte loads (sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2> or sycl::vec<uint32_t, 4>) for loading quantization blocks from global memory. Currently all loads are scalar 4-byte via get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned. Wider loads reduce the number of memory transactions and better utilize the memory bus.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement in memory throughput for the weight loading phase. Impact is higher for simpler formats (Q4_0, Q8_0) where the quant data is more regular.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In vecdotq.hpp vec_dot functions, replace pairs of sequential get_int calls with a single sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2> load. For Q4_0: currently loads v.x and v.y separately — load as sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2>. Must verify 8-byte alignment of quantization block qs fields. The reordered layout (contiguous quants) is more amenable to vectorization than the AoS layout.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements must be verified per format. IQ formats have irregular layouts that may not support aligned wide loads. Need to handle the tail case when the quant data size is not a multiple of the vector width.

optimization_opportunities.description: Extend the reordered (SoA) data layout support from the current 3 formats (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K) to all commonly-used quantization formats, particularly Q8_0, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q4_1, Q2_K, Q3_K, Q5_K. The reordered layout separates quant bytes from scale factors into contiguous regions, enabling coalesced memory access patterns that dramatically improve memory bandwidth utilization.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement for each newly-supported format. The existing Q4_0/Q4_K/Q6_K reordered paths demonstrate the performance benefit. Most LLM models use Q4_K or Q6_K, but Q8_0 and Q5_K are also common.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each new format: 1) Add reorder_tensor support in quants.hpp/cpp (SoA packing). 2) Implement reorder_mul_mat_vec_<fmt>_q8_1_sycl launcher. 3) Implement the reordered kernel using block_type::get_block_offset(). 4) Wire into the dispatch switch in ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_vec_q. The existing Q4_0 reorder implementation serves as a template.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Each format has a different block structure, so the reordering logic must be format-specific. Complex formats like Q3_K and Q5_K have multiple sub-fields (qs, qh, scales, d) that all need separate contiguous regions. Must ensure the reorder/dereorder is compatible with other kernel paths that may access the same tensor.

optimization_opportunities.description: Enable GGML_SYCL_F16 build flag to use half-precision arithmetic for scale factor multiplication in vec_dot functions. Several vecdotq.hpp functions (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1) have conditional FP16 paths under #ifdef GGML_SYCL_F16 that perform dm4 * ds8 in half precision before converting to float.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% for applicable formats. FP16 compute is 2x faster than FP32 on Xe2. However, the scale multiplication is a small fraction of the total compute (dominated by dp4a integer ops), so the overall impact is modest.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON to the CMake build flags. Verify numerical accuracy by running the full test suite with this flag enabled. The GGML_SYCL_F16 paths in vecdotq.hpp (lines ~532, ~614, ~666) are already implemented but disabled by default.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: FP16 has lower precision (~3.3 decimal digits vs ~7 for FP32). For some quantization formats with large scale factors, the reduced precision could introduce noticeable numerical errors. Must validate with accuracy tests, especially for larger models.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT artifacts: replace dpct::dp4a with sycl::vec<int8_t,4> dot product or direct dp4a intrinsic, replace dpct::vectorized_binary with standard SYCL vector operations, remove DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP guards, replace __dpct_inline__ with standard inline hints.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minimal direct performance impact. Primarily a code quality and maintainability improvement. May enable better compiler optimization by using standard SYCL constructs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1) dpct::dp4a -> use sycl::dot() on char4 types or keep the dp4a helper but move it out of dpct namespace. 2) dpct::vectorized_binary -> use sycl::vec operations. 3) Remove DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP checks (always true for Intel). 4) __dpct_inline__ -> inline or SYCL_EXTERNAL. 5) dpct::queue_ptr -> sycl::queue*.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward refactoring. Each replacement can be tested independently. No algorithmic changes.

kernels.efficiency_notes: MMVQ is inherently memory-bandwidth bound (arithmetic intensity ~0.5 ops/byte for Q4 formats vs the 27 ops/byte compute intensity threshold). The key to performance is maximizing memory bandwidth utilization. The legacy kernel path (17 of 20 formats) uses only 16 work-items per work-group — a severe occupancy limitation on Intel GPUs. The reordered kernels (3 formats) are much better at 256 work-items and SoA layout, but still miss SLM caching of the shared Y vector. The kernel is critical for single-token inference (autoregressive decoding), where the matrix is weights and the vector is the hidden state — this path dominates inference latency.

kernels.name: dequantize_mul_mat_vec (DMMV)

launch_config.global_size_expression: Generic: (1, 1, nrows/GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y) * (1, 1, WARP_SIZE). K-quant: (1, ny, nrows) * (1, ny, QK_WARP_SIZE)
launch_config.notes: Two distinct launch families. Generic kernels (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, F16) use work-group size 16 (1 sub-group of WARP_SIZE=16). K-quant kernels (Q2_K through Q6_K) use QK_WARP_SIZE=32 with [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(32)]] — CRITICAL: requesting sub-group size 32 on Intel where native width is 16. Both families are far below the recommended 256-512 work-group size. 3D nd_range with unused dimensions (CUDA artifact).

strided_accesses: Generic: adjacent threads access blocks spaced vals_per_iter columns apart — strided, not coalesced across blocks
Generic: Y vector accessed with stride of vals_per_iter between adjacent threads
K-quant: AoS block layout means quantization block fields (qs, scales, hmask, d) are interleaved — strided access to each field
K-quant: Y vector accessed with large strides (16, 32, 48, ..., 128 elements from base) — very poor spatial locality
memory_patterns.notes: All loads are scalar 4-byte or smaller via get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned helpers or direct byte/half loads. No sycl::vec types for memory loads. The reorder variant (Q4_0 only) separates scales from quant data for better access locality but still uses scalar loads.

slm_usage.notes: Zero SLM used in any DMMV kernel variant. All reduction via sub-group shuffles. No cross-sub-group communication mechanism. This means no Y vector sharing across sub-groups in a work-group, and limits the effective work-group size to 1 sub-group for the generic kernels.

reduction_pattern.reduction_details: All kernels use manual butterfly reduction via dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor (DPCT artifact of CUDA __shfl_xor_sync). Generic kernel: log2(WARP_SIZE) iterations with mask starting at WARP_SIZE/2 or WARP_SIZE/4. K-quant kernels: log2(QK_WARP_SIZE)=5 iterations — the mask=16 iteration XORs beyond sub-group width 16 on Intel, producing undefined/identity values. This is a latent correctness issue for K-quant kernels on Intel GPUs.

data_types.accumulator_type: float (dfloat when GGML_SYCL_F16 is set: sycl::half)
data_types.dot_product_type: float multiply-accumulate (no dp4a — dequantize first, then float mul-add)
data_types.notes: Default path uses float32 for all compute. GGML_SYCL_F16 compile flag enables half-precision accumulation for generic kernels only — K-quant kernels always use float32 regardless of flag. No integer dot products (dp4a) — unlike MMVQ/MMQ, DMMV dequantizes to float first then multiplies. This is inherently less compute-efficient than fused quantized multiply paths.

functions: sycl::fma (in dequantize helpers for Q4_1, Q5_1)
math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions. All compute is bit manipulation (dequantization) followed by float multiply-accumulate. sycl::fma used in some dequantize helpers.

hot_loops: Generic outer loop (line 47): iterates ncols/64 times, NOT unrolled (dynamic trip count)
Generic inner loop (line 55): 2 iterations on Intel (vals_per_iter=4, step=2), UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Reorder outer loop (line 122): iterates ncols/512 times, NOT unrolled
Reorder inner loop (line 129): 16 iterations on Intel (vals_per_iter=32, step=2), UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
K-quant block loop (e.g., Q2_K line 266): iterates num_blocks_per_row times, NOT unrolled
K-quant inner computation: small fixed-count loops (1-4 iterations) over K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION — NOT explicitly unrolled in most K-quant kernels
loop_analysis.notes: Only the generic/reorder inner loops and reduction loops have #pragma unroll. K-quant computation inner loops are NOT marked with #pragma unroll, despite having small fixed trip counts that would benefit from unrolling.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: DMMV is a matrix-vector product — inherently memory-bandwidth bound. Arithmetic intensity is ~1 op/byte for dequantize+multiply (even lower than fused MMVQ since DMMV dequantizes to float first, doubling the intermediate data width). With Intel's compute intensity threshold at ~27 ops/byte, DMMV needs maximum bandwidth utilization. The tiny work-group sizes (16 or 64), strided memory access, and no SLM caching severely limit actual bandwidth achieved.
anti_patterns: CRITICAL: K-quant kernels request [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(32)]] (QK_WARP_SIZE=32) on Intel where native sub-group width is 16 — correctness risk with butterfly reduction reaching beyond actual sub-group boundaries
Generic kernels: work-group size of 16 (1 sub-group) — far below Intel's recommended 256-512
K-quant kernels: work-group size of 64 (2 rows * 32 threads) — still below recommended
3D nd_range with 2 unused dimensions — CUDA migration artifact, should be 1D
dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reduction instead of sycl::reduce_over_group — DPCT artifact
dpct::has_capability_or_fail(fp16) called even when F16 is not used for computation
dpct::queue_ptr, item_ct1, __dpct_inline__ naming — DPCT artifacts throughout
DPCT1110 register pressure warning comments preserved in source (lines 220-226, 346-352, etc.)
No vectorized loads — all scalar byte/int loads
No SLM caching of Y vector — each sub-group independently loads Y from global memory
Strided memory access patterns for both weight and Y vector loads
Off-by-one: K-quant kernels use 'row > nrows' instead of 'row >= nrows' (likely benign due to grid sizing)
Reorder support limited to Q4_0 only — other formats stuck with AoS layout
GGML_SYCL_F16 half-precision path not applied to K-quant kernels

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix K-quant sub-group size mismatch: QK_WARP_SIZE=32 is hard-coded in presets.hpp but Intel native sub-group size is 16. The K-quant kernels request [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(32)]] and perform butterfly reduction with masks up to 16, which exceeds the actual sub-group width. Either: (a) rewrite K-quant kernels to use WARP_SIZE=16 sub-groups with adjusted indexing, or (b) restructure to use 2 cooperating sub-groups of 16 with SLM-based inter-sub-group reduction. Option (a) is simpler and aligns with MMVQ's approach.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness fix — ensures K-quant DMMV produces correct results on Intel GPUs. May also improve performance by 10-20% by running at native SIMD16 width instead of emulated SIMD32.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In presets.hpp, make QK_WARP_SIZE equal to GGML_SYCL_WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel). Adjust K-quant kernel indexing: tid = item_ct1.get_local_id(2) % 16 (was %32). Each thread processes more elements per row to compensate for fewer threads. Adjust reduction to log2(16)=4 iterations. Change [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(QK_WARP_SIZE)]] to use 16. Adjust ny (number of rows per work-group) and grid dimensions accordingly.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires restructuring the data access patterns in all 5 K-quant kernels (Q2_K through Q6_K). Each has format-specific bit manipulation that assumes 32 lanes. Extensive testing needed for all K-quant formats.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 16 (generic) or 64 (K-quant) to 256 by grouping 16 sub-groups per work-group. Each sub-group independently computes one row's dot product. This is the same optimization as opt_002_001 for MMVQ and has been proven to work in the MMVQ reordered kernels. Current single-sub-group work-groups severely underutilize Intel GPU occupancy.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 25-50% throughput improvement from better occupancy, memory-level parallelism, and hardware thread utilization. The B60 has 64 hardware threads per Xe-core; with 16-thread work-groups, only 1 work-group occupies 1 hardware thread slot.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change block_dims from (1,1,WARP_SIZE) to (1,1,num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE) with num_subgroups=16. Each sub-group uses sub_group_id to compute a different row. Adjust grid to block_num_y = ceil(nrows / num_subgroups). The MMVQ reordered kernels (mmvq.cpp lines 537-554) serve as a proven template. For K-quant kernels, first fix the sub-group size issue (opt_003_001), then apply the same multi-sub-group pattern.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Sub-groups are independent (each computes a different row), so grouping them is straightforward. Only risk is if nrows < num_subgroups — need bounds checking (row < nrows guard).

optimization_opportunities.description: Cache Y vector in SLM for multi-sub-group work-groups. When 16 sub-groups in one work-group all compute dot products against the same Y vector, each sub-group currently redundantly loads Y from global memory (16x bandwidth waste). Load Y into SLM once per work-group, then all sub-groups read from SLM. For DMMV which is purely memory-bandwidth bound, this is a critical optimization.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-35% overall throughput improvement. Y vector typically occupies ncols*sizeof(float) bytes (e.g., 4096*4=16KB for a 4096-column matrix) — fits well within the 64KB SLM budget. The weight matrix bandwidth is unchanged, but Y bandwidth drops by ~16x.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Allocate sycl::local_accessor<float, 1>(ncols, h) for Y data. Have all sub-groups cooperatively load Y into SLM (each sub-group loads ncols/num_subgroups elements). Insert group_barrier(). Then all sub-groups read Y from SLM. For matrices wider than ~16K columns, use tiled loading (load a chunk of Y into SLM per iteration). Depends on opt_003_002 (multi-sub-group work-groups).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: SLM allocation size depends on ncols — must handle dynamically sized matrices. For very wide matrices (ncols > 16K), SLM cannot hold entire Y vector — need tiled approach with barriers per tile. The barrier overhead must not exceed the bandwidth savings.

optimization_opportunities.description: Extend reorder (SoA) layout support from Q4_0 only to all commonly-used quantization formats. The current AoS (array-of-structures) layout interleaves quantization fields (qs, d, scales, qh) within each block, causing strided access patterns. The SoA layout stores all qs bytes contiguously, all scales contiguously, etc., enabling coalesced reads where adjacent threads access adjacent memory addresses.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% throughput improvement per format. The Q4_0 reorder variant in dmmv.cpp already demonstrates this pattern. Extending to Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0 is straightforward; K-quant formats (Q2_K-Q6_K) are more complex due to multi-level scales.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each format: 1) Add reorder_tensor support in quants.hpp/cpp (SoA packing for the format's fields). 2) Implement dequantize_mul_mat_vec_reorder template instantiation or hand-coded reorder kernel. 3) Wire into the dispatcher switch in ggml_sycl_op_dequantize_mul_mat_vec. The existing Q4_0 reorder implementation (dmmv.cpp lines 93-197) serves as the template. Priority: Q8_0 and Q4_1 first (simple block structures), then K-quant formats.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Each format has a different block structure requiring format-specific reorder logic. Must ensure reorder/dereorder is compatible with other kernel paths. K-quant formats have multi-level scales that complicate the SoA layout.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace all dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reductions with sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, sycl::plus<float>()). This applies to both generic kernels (~3 instances) and K-quant kernels (~5 instances). The manual butterfly reduction is a DPCT artifact and may not compile to optimal code on Intel GPUs.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% improvement. The compiler can generate optimal reduction code from the high-level reduce_over_group API. More importantly, this eliminates the DPCT dependency and fixes the correctness issue where K-quant butterfly reductions exceed sub-group width.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace each '#pragma unroll for (mask = ...; mask > 0; mask >>= 1) { tmp += dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor(..., tmp, mask); }' block with 'tmp = sycl::reduce_over_group(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, sycl::plus<float>());'. This is the same fix as opt_002_003 for MMVQ. Approximately 8 replacement sites across the file.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Direct replacement with standard SYCL API. sycl::reduce_over_group handles the sub-group width automatically, fixing the QK_WARP_SIZE=32 vs actual-size=16 mismatch.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 8-byte or 16-byte loads (sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2> or sycl::vec<uint32_t, 4>) for loading quantization blocks and Y vector from global memory. Currently all loads are scalar (1 or 4 bytes). Wider loads reduce memory transactions and better utilize the memory bus width. Particularly impactful for the Y vector which is float32 and easily amenable to vec4 loads.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement in memory throughput. Y vector vec4 loads (16 bytes each) would reduce Y memory transactions by 4x. Weight loads benefit varies by format — simpler formats (Q4_0, Q8_0) benefit more.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For Y vector: replace sequential y[idx], y[idx+1], ... with sycl::vec<float,4> loads via reinterpret_cast. For weights: format-specific — Q8_0 has contiguous qs bytes amenable to vec4 loads; Q4_0 can load 2 bytes as a single short. Must verify alignment requirements. The reorder variant's contiguous data layout is more amenable to vectorization.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements must be verified. The Y vector (float array) should be naturally 4-byte aligned but may not be 16-byte aligned for vec4. Use __attribute__((aligned(16))) or runtime alignment checks.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to K-quant inner computation loops. The K-quant kernels (Q2_K through Q6_K) have small fixed-count inner loops (1-4 iterations) that are not explicitly unrolled, unlike the generic kernel's inner loop which has #pragma unroll. Unrolling these constant-trip-count loops eliminates loop overhead and enables better instruction scheduling.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-7% improvement. The inner loops are small (1-4 iterations) so the loop overhead is proportionally significant. Combined effect across all K-quant formats.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add #pragma unroll before the inner computation loops in each K-quant kernel: Q2_K (line ~281), Q3_K (line ~411), Q4_K (line ~522), Q5_K (line ~667), Q6_K (line ~813). These loops iterate K_QUANTS_PER_ITERATION or fixed constants. Only unroll the innermost computation loops, not the outer block iteration loop (dynamic trip count).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Minimal risk — unrolling small constant-count loops is a standard optimization. May slightly increase register pressure but the loops are very small.

optimization_opportunities.description: Enable GGML_SYCL_F16 by default and extend half-precision support to K-quant kernels. The generic kernels already have half-precision paths under the GGML_SYCL_F16 flag, but K-quant kernels always use float32. On Intel Xe2, FP16 compute is 2x faster than FP32, so using half-precision for the multiply-accumulate phase would double the effective compute throughput.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% overall improvement. DMMV is memory-bound, so compute speedup has limited impact. But for wider matrices where compute becomes more significant, FP16 accumulation helps. K-quant formats have enough precision in their scales that FP16 accumulation should not introduce meaningful errors.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1) Add -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON to default CMake build flags. 2) For K-quant kernels, change accumulator from float to sycl::half and use half-precision multiply-accumulate. 3) Convert final reduction result back to float for output. Must validate numerical accuracy with full test suite.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: FP16 has ~3.3 decimal digits of precision vs ~7 for FP32. For long rows (large ncols), accumulation error may grow. Need to test with large models (7B+ parameters) to verify accuracy is acceptable. May need Kahan summation or periodic float32 accumulation for long rows.

kernels.efficiency_notes: DMMV is a fallback path for matrix-vector multiplication when the fused MMVQ path is not available or not optimal. It dequantizes to float first then multiplies, which is inherently less efficient than MMVQ's fused quantized dot product. The kernel has severe issues: K-quant sub-group size mismatch (QK_WARP_SIZE=32 on Intel native SIMD16), tiny work-group sizes (16 or 64), no SLM caching, no vectorized loads, strided memory access, and extensive DPCT artifacts. On the B60, memory bandwidth is the bottleneck (~0.5-1 ops/byte arithmetic intensity vs 27 ops/byte threshold), so maximizing bandwidth utilization through coalesced access, vectorized loads, and Y vector caching is critical. The kernel is used for single-token inference with quantized models.

kernels.name: dequantize_block_sycl (convert)

launch_config.global_size_expression: Varies by format: nb * work_group_size for most, where nb = number of quantization blocks
launch_config.notes: 22+ distinct kernel launch configurations. Almost all use nd_range<3> with (1,1,N) — a DPCT artifact (only q4_K_reorder uses correct nd_range<1>). Only q4_0_reorder specifies [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. Work-group sizes range from 16 (q4_0_reorder) to 256 (generic path). The generic path (WG=256) handles Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0 via dispatch table; specialized paths use 32 or 64.

strided_accesses: Generic dequantize_block: writes 2 elements per thread at y[iybs+iqs] and y[iybs+iqs+y_offset] — the second write is strided by qk/2
Q2_K, Q6_K: output writes at strides of 32 (y[l+0], y[l+32], y[l+64], y[l+96])
Q3_K: writes at stride 1 within a 4-element span but overall block-strided
Q5_K: writes at offsets y[0], y[1], y[32], y[33] — partial stride
AoS block layout for non-reorder kernels: interleaved qs/d/scales fields cause strided reads
memory_patterns.vectorization_notes: Only Q4_K and Q4_K_reorder use vectorized loads via vec_aligned_load<uint8_t, 4> (4-byte vector load). Generic path uses dfloat2 (sycl::float2 or sycl::half2) for 2-element output. All other kernels use scalar loads (1-4 bytes via type casting).

slm_usage.notes: Only Q4_K and Q4_K_reorder use SLM: 12 bytes for scale data loaded cooperatively by first 12 threads. All other kernels (20+) use no SLM at all. The 12-byte SLM usage is trivial relative to the 64KB available — massive underutilization.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reductions anywhere. All kernels are pure map operations — each thread independently dequantizes a subset of elements with no inter-thread data exchange (except Q4_K's cooperative scale loading).

data_types.scale_type: sycl::half for block scales, converted to float for computation
data_types.notes: The generic path supports half-precision computation via dfloat typedef (sycl::half when GGML_SYCL_F16 is defined). Specialized K-quant kernels always use float32 for intermediate computation. Output type is templated (float or half). No opportunity for joint_matrix since these are pure dequantization (no matrix multiply).

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions. All operations are bit manipulation (shift, mask, AND, OR) followed by scale multiplication and bias addition. sycl::fma used in Q4_1 and Q5_1 for fused multiply-add of scale+minimum.

hot_loops: Q4_0 specialized: for (l=0; l<4; l++) — NOT unrolled
Q4_0 reorder: for (l=0; l<QK4_0/2; l++) = 16 iterations — UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Q3_K: for (l=l0; l<l0+4; l++) — NOT unrolled
Q4_K: for (l=0; l<n; l++) where n=4 — NOT unrolled
IQ1_S/IQ1_M: for (j=0; j<8; j++) — UNROLLED
IQ2_S/IQ3_S: for (j=0; j<8; j++) — UNROLLED
IQ2_XXS/IQ2_XS/IQ3_XXS: for (j=0; j<8; j++) — NOT unrolled
IQ4_NL/IQ4_XS: for (j=0; j<4; j++) — UNROLLED
MXFP4: for (j=0; j<4; j++) — NOT unrolled
convert_unary_nc: grid-stride loop — UNROLLED
loop_analysis.notes: Inconsistent unrolling: some format-specific kernels have #pragma unroll, others with identical loop structures do not. All loops have small constant trip counts (4-16) and would benefit from unrolling.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Dequantization is purely memory-bandwidth bound: each input byte produces 2-8 output float/half values via bit manipulation (trivial compute). The arithmetic intensity is well below the B60's 27 ops/byte threshold. Performance depends entirely on memory bandwidth utilization — coalesced reads of quantized data and coalesced writes of output. The strided output patterns and small work-group sizes limit achieved bandwidth.
anti_patterns: Pervasive nd_range<3> with (1,1,N) — DPCT artifact. Only q4_K_reorder correctly uses nd_range<1>
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size()]] on 20+ of 22 kernel variants — only q4_0_reorder has it
dpct::has_capability_or_fail called on every kernel launch — DPCT runtime check artifact
__dpct_inline__ annotations in dequantize.hpp — DPCT artifact, should be standard inline
Inconsistent work-group sizes: 16 (q4_0_reorder), 32 (most specialized), 64 (K-quants), 256 (generic) — no clear rationale for Intel GPUs
Inconsistent loop unrolling: some kernels have #pragma unroll, identical structures don't
Inconsistent reorder kernel conventions: q4_0_reorder uses nd_range<3>+reqd_sub_group_size, q4_K_reorder uses nd_range<1>, q6_K_reorder uses nd_range<3> — three different patterns
Dispatch table inconsistency: Q4_0 FP16 path uses generic WG=256 kernel, FP32 path uses specialized WG=32 kernel
No vectorized loads except Q4_K (vec_aligned_load<uint8_t,4>) — all other formats use scalar byte loads
Strided output writes (stride 32) in Q2_K, Q5_K, Q6_K reduce coalescing efficiency
IQ format kernels use global memory lookup tables (iq2xxs_grid, iq3xxs_grid, etc.) — scattered random reads, no SLM caching of tables

optimization_opportunities.description: Standardize work-group sizes to 256 across all dequantization kernels. Currently sizes vary from 16 to 256 with no clear rationale for Intel GPUs. With WG=256, each Xe-core gets 256/16=16 sub-groups per work-group for better occupancy. The generic dequantize_block template already uses 256 successfully — apply the same to all specialized kernels by having each thread process more elements (e.g., for Q4_0: change from 32 threads * 8 elements to 256 threads * 1 element, or better yet 256 threads * 4 elements for higher throughput).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% throughput improvement for kernels currently using WG=32 or WG=64, from better occupancy and latency hiding on the B60's 20 Xe-cores. The improvement is larger for small tensors where fewer work-groups are launched.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each format-specific launcher: change the block size from 32 or 64 to 256. Adjust the per-thread element count and grid dimensions accordingly. Example for Q4_0: nb_blocks = (k / QK4_0); launch with nd_range<1>(nb_blocks * 256 / new_blocks_per_wg, 256). Each thread processes k/256 elements instead of k/32. The Q4_K_reorder kernel (already nd_range<1>, WG=32) is the easiest to increase. Ensure total work is unchanged.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure map kernels with no inter-thread dependencies — increasing work-group size just changes scheduling granularity. Only risk is if register pressure increases from processing more elements per thread, but dequantization uses very few registers.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized memory loads (sycl::vec<uint8_t, 8> or sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2>) for reading quantized data, and vectorized stores (sycl::vec<float, 4> or sycl::vec<sycl::half, 8>) for writing dequantized output. Currently only Q4_K uses vec_aligned_load<uint8_t, 4> — all other formats use scalar 1-4 byte loads. For a purely memory-bound kernel, maximizing bytes per transaction is critical. Vectorized loads/stores reduce memory transactions by 2-4x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement. Dequantization is purely bandwidth-limited — each byte of input produces 2-8 bytes of output. Wider loads/stores directly translate to higher effective bandwidth. For float output, vec4 stores (16 bytes) instead of scalar stores (4 bytes) reduce store transactions by 4x.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For output writes: accumulate 4 float results into a sycl::vec<float, 4> and write via a single aligned store. For input reads: load quantized bytes as sycl::vec<uint8_t, N> where N matches the quant block's qs field alignment. The reorder (SoA) data layout is more amenable to wide loads since qs bytes are contiguous. Priority: Q4_0 (most common), Q8_0, Q6_K, Q4_K (already partially done). Must ensure 16-byte alignment for vec4 float stores.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements may not always be met. Output buffer alignment depends on the caller. Input quantization blocks may have sub-4-byte alignment for some fields. Need to handle tail cases where element count is not a multiple of the vector width.

optimization_opportunities.description: Eliminate strided output writes in Q2_K, Q5_K, Q6_K dequantization. These kernels write 4 elements at stride 32 (y[l+0], y[l+32], y[l+64], y[l+96]), meaning 32 threads each write to non-adjacent locations. Restructure thread indexing so adjacent threads write to adjacent output locations. This requires changing how threads map to elements within a quant block — instead of each thread handling elements at stride-32, use a transposed mapping where a group of 4 adjacent threads handles 4 contiguous elements.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-25% improvement for affected formats (Q2_K, Q5_K, Q6_K). Coalesced writes generate fewer memory transactions (16 adjacent float writes = 1 cache line store vs 16 scattered writes = up to 16 separate transactions). Q6_K is particularly common in K-quant models.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For Q6_K (64 threads, 256 elements per block, 4 elements per thread): currently thread tid writes y[off+0], y[off+32], y[off+64], y[off+96]. Remap so threads 0-3 write y[0..3], threads 4-7 write y[4..7], etc. This means changing from tid->(4 elements at stride 32) to tid->(4 contiguous elements at offset tid*4). The dequantization logic must be adjusted to fetch the correct input bits for the new thread-to-element mapping. This is a non-trivial restructuring of the bit manipulation code.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The complex bit manipulation in K-quant dequantization makes thread remapping non-trivial. Each format has unique bit packing. Must carefully verify correctness for all edge cases. The restructured code may be harder to maintain.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to all inner loops that are missing it. Currently only ~10 of ~20 format-specific kernels have #pragma unroll on their inner loops, despite all having small constant trip counts (4-16 iterations). The missing kernels include Q4_0, Q4_1, Q3_K, Q4_K, IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ3_XXS, and MXFP4.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement per affected kernel. Loop overhead (branch, increment) is significant when the loop body is only 2-4 instructions. For a 4-iteration loop, eliminating overhead saves ~20% of loop cycles. For memory-bound kernels, the freed instruction slots allow better overlap of memory operations.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add #pragma unroll before each undecorated for loop in dequantize.hpp: Q4_0 specialized (~line 189), Q4_1 (~line 248), Q3_K (~line 323), Q4_K_common (~line 376), IQ2_XXS (~line 594), IQ2_XS (~line 620), IQ3_XXS (~line 675), MXFP4 (~line 835). Verify that trip counts are compile-time constants (they are — all use literal constants like 4, 8, 16).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adding #pragma unroll to small constant-trip-count loops is a safe, well-understood optimization. Worst case: compiler already unrolls and the pragma is redundant. No correctness risk.

optimization_opportunities.description: Cache IQ format lookup tables (iq2xxs_grid, iq3xxs_grid, iq3s_grid, iq2xs_grid, ksigns_iq2xs, kvalues_iq4nl) in SLM for IQ dequantization kernels. These tables are accessed via random/scattered reads from global memory, incurring cache misses and high latency. Loading frequently-used table entries into SLM would provide predictable low-latency access. Tables are small: iq2xxs_grid = 256*uint32_t = 1KB, kvalues_iq4nl = 16*float = 64 bytes.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% improvement for IQ format dequantization. The lookup tables cause random global memory access patterns that defeat the L1 cache's line-based prefetching. SLM provides deterministic single-cycle access. The improvement depends on what fraction of kernel time is spent in table lookups vs output writes.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each IQ kernel: allocate sycl::local_accessor for the table (e.g., 256 uint32_t entries for iq2xxs_grid = 1KB). Have work-group cooperatively load the table into SLM (each thread loads table_size/WG entries). Insert group_barrier(). Then replace global table reads with SLM reads. Requires increasing work-group size to at least 256 to enable efficient cooperative loading (pairs with opt_004_001). Total SLM per work-group: ~1-2KB for the largest table, well within 64KB limit.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Lookup tables are read-only and small. SLM caching is a standard optimization pattern. The barrier cost is incurred once per kernel invocation, amortized across all table lookups. Only risk is if the table is too large for SLM (none are — largest is ~1KB).

optimization_opportunities.description: Convert all nd_range<3>(sycl::range<3>(1,1,N), sycl::range<3>(1,1,WG)) launches to nd_range<1>(N, WG). The 3D launches with trivial first two dimensions are DPCT migration artifacts from CUDA's 3D grid/block model. Using nd_range<1> is cleaner, may avoid trivial scheduling overhead for unused dimensions, and aligns with the kernel's actual 1D nature. The q4_K_reorder kernel already demonstrates the correct nd_range<1> pattern.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-3% improvement. Primarily a code quality fix. May provide marginal improvement from simpler index computation (get_global_id(0) vs get_global_id(2)).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In each launcher function: replace sycl::nd_range<3>(sycl::range<3>(1,1,global), sycl::range<3>(1,1,local)) with sycl::nd_range<1>(global, local). In each kernel: replace item.get_global_id(2) with item.get_global_id(0), item.get_local_id(2) with item.get_local_id(0), item.get_group(2) with item.get_group(0). The q4_K_reorder kernel (convert.cpp:194-209) serves as the template. Approximately 20 launch sites to update.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure mechanical refactoring. No algorithmic change. The nd_range<1> pattern is proven by q4_K_reorder.

optimization_opportunities.description: Extend reorder (SoA) data layout support from Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K to all commonly-used quantization formats for the dequantization path. The SoA layout separates quantization block fields (qs, scales, d) into contiguous regions, enabling coalesced reads where adjacent threads access adjacent memory addresses. Currently only 3 formats have reorder kernels in convert.cpp.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement per newly-supported format. The reorder layout enables coalesced reads of qs bytes (the dominant memory access), reducing cache line waste from the interleaved AoS layout. Combined with vectorized loads (opt_004_002), this could achieve near-peak bandwidth.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each new format: implement a dequantize_block_*_reorder function in dequantize.hpp that reads from separated qs/scales/d regions using offsets computed from the block index. Add a corresponding dequantize_row_*_sycl_reorder launcher in convert.cpp. Wire into the dispatch tables with is_reorder checks. Priority: Q8_0 (simple, common), Q4_1 (simple), Q5_K (common in K-quant models). The existing Q4_0_reorder, Q4_K_reorder, Q6_K_reorder implementations serve as templates.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Each format has unique block structure. The reorder/dereorder packing must be format-specific and consistent with the quants.hpp reorder infrastructure. Must ensure compatibility with all other kernel paths that may access the same tensor data.

optimization_opportunities.description: Remove dpct::has_capability_or_fail runtime checks from every kernel launch. These DPCT artifact calls check sycl::aspect::fp16 capability at every submission, adding unnecessary overhead. The check should be performed once during device initialization and cached, or removed entirely since the B60 always supports FP16.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-2% improvement in kernel launch overhead. More impactful when many small dequantization kernels are launched in succession (e.g., during model loading or layer-by-layer inference).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Remove all dpct::has_capability_or_fail(dpct::get_current_device(), {sycl::aspect::fp16}) calls from convert.cpp (approximately 20 sites). If a runtime check is desired, perform it once in the SYCL backend initialization and store the result. Also remove the associated DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP macro guards.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The B60 always supports FP16. Removing the check is safe for the target hardware. For portability, a one-time initialization check could replace the per-launch check.

kernels.efficiency_notes: Dequantization is a pure map operation (no reductions, no inter-thread communication) that is entirely memory-bandwidth bound. The arithmetic intensity is trivially low (~0.1-0.5 ops/byte for bit manipulation + scale multiply). The kernel's efficiency depends solely on memory bandwidth utilization. Current issues: inconsistent work-group sizes (16-256), strided output writes in K-quant formats, mostly scalar loads (no vectorization except Q4_K), pervasive DPCT artifacts. The kernel is called frequently during inference (every matmul path that dequantizes before compute) but is not on the critical path for single-token latency — it's used more during prompt processing and as a utility for other ops. Optimization potential is medium because: (a) the kernel is already functional and not as severely impacted as MMVQ/DMMV by tiny work-groups (the generic path uses WG=256), (b) the primary bottleneck is memory bandwidth which is harder to improve without algorithmic changes, and (c) some formats already have reorder+vectorized paths.
